relationship_to_restored_text: Interpretive contemplative layer aligned by verse. This does not replace the source-audited restored translation.

verses.mystical_translation: Seventy royal sons become leverage in Jehu's letters.
He reminds Samaria's officials that they possess the machinery of rule.
They are invited to choose a king and fight, knowing the threat behind the invitation.
Fear answers before deliberation can begin.
Officials surrender their judgment to Jehu.
His second letter demands the heads of the sons they were charged to protect.
Seventy dependent lives are slaughtered and packed into baskets.
The heads are displayed at the gate as political theater.
Jehu disperses blame for the horror he orchestrated.
Prophetic fulfillment is invoked over the heaps.
The purge expands through Ahab's household, officials, allies, and priests.
Jehu moves toward Samaria.
Relatives of Ahaziah identify themselves while traveling toward the royal household.
They are seized alive and killed at a pit without trial.
Jehonadab's hand joins Jehu's chariot.
Jehu asks another man to witness his zeal.
The remaining house of Ahab in Samaria is destroyed.
Jehu announces greater devotion to Baal as bait.
A sacred gathering is turned into a death trap.
The assembly is proclaimed as holy.
The house fills with worshippers who do not know they have been selected for slaughter.
Religious garments become targeting markers.
Identity is sorted so no servant of YHWH remains among those marked.
Armed guards are threatened with death if anyone escapes.
The doors close behind worship, and swords enter.
Sacred pillars are dragged out and burned.
The temple is demolished and turned into a place of humiliation.
The narrator calls Baal destroyed from Israel.
Yet Jehu preserves the royal worship system at Bethel and Dan.
His dynasty is rewarded inside the narrative's own troubled theology.
The same text says his heart never fully walked in Torah.
Israel's territory begins shrinking under Hazael.
Gilead, Gad, Reuben, Manasseh, and Bashan are cut away.
Jehu's power is archived in royal records.
He dies and passes the throne to Jehoahaz.
Twenty-eight years close a reign built through terror and partial reform.

contemplative_note: 2 Kings 10 is the nightmare of reform without moral limits. Jehu destroys one abusive order by coercing guardians, killing children and kin, trapping worshippers, and weaponizing clothing and sacred space. Zeal without due process becomes terror wearing religious language.
